title: Introduction
text: Binary search is one of the most fundamental algorithms in programming.
It is a searching algorithm used to find a particular value in a sorted collection, such as an array.
Instead of checking every element one at a time, it repeatedly examines the middle element and uses that comparison to decide which half of the collection could contain the target.
This allows binary search to find values much more efficiently than a linear search if the required conditions are met.

title: How it works
text: Instead of iterating through every element one by one, binary search exploits an attribute called monotonicity.
It begins by looking at the middle element of the sorted array. If the middle element is the target, the search is complete.
If the target is greater than the middle element, the algorithm continues searching only the right half because every value on the left is guaranteed to be too small.
If the target is smaller, it searches only the left half following the same principle. The process repeats until the target is found or no elements remain.
Because half of the remaining elements are removed after every comparison, binary search takes logarithmic time, written as O(log n).
For example, in an array of size 1'000'000'000, binary search checks at most about 30 elements, which is significantly fewer than 1'000'000'000.

title: When to use it
text: Binary search can only be used when the data is ordered in a way that lets us eliminate half of the search space after each comparison.
The most common example is a sorted array of numbers, where smaller values appear before larger values.
The collection should also allow direct access to its middle elements.
Binary search is useful when searching through a large, already sorted collection.
It cannot be applied directly to an unsorted array. The data must be sorted first.

title: Common Variations
text:
This website taught you the basics of the 'standard' binary search.
 However, it is important to note that while this is the most basic application of binary search, most problems cannot be solved by it.
 All binary search problems can be reduced to 2 underlying structures: first-true and last-true.
 The 'standard' binary search that finds an existing value in a sorted array, is really just a modified lower bound binary search.
 Below you can read a little about the more relevant and practical versions of binary search.

title: Lower Bound
text:
One of the most common applications of binary search, is finding the first true value in a monotone answer space.
 This will always be the first value satisfying some condition, iff that condition follows a FFFFTTTT pattern.
 One application would be trying to repeatedly find the least amount of days needed to complete a task that requires X units of time, where each day you can use time[i] amount of time.
 Instead of looping through the entire array for each X, which takes O(n) per query, giving O(n * q), we precompute the prefix sum* of the time array, and use lower bound binary search to find the first day / index, where the accumulated time >= X.
 Now we have reduced the time complexity to O(q log n), which is significantly better, especially for large input.

title: Upper Bound
text:
The counterpart to lower bound binary search is upper bound binary search.
 It answers the question: What is the last value that still satisfies a condition?
 Recall that this also only works in a monotone answer space.
 The answer must follow a TTTTFFFF pattern, and will not work without monotonicity.
 An example of its application would be repeatedly finding the most number of money one can earn in n days, if we are not allowed to earn more than X currency units.
 As you may have noticed, binary search is oftentimes paired with other techniques, especially for the check function.
 Here the naive bruteforce would be manually iterating and keeping a running sum until it exceeds our limit.
 Again, it would take O(n) operations, and is less than favorable if input is large.
 Upper bound can find the answer in less than 31 operations, given a reasonable input size.
